title: Caesar's coin (Mark 12:13–17)
hookLine: whose image is on it? give Caesar his, and God what is God's

lines: AN ODD PAIR, SENT TO CATCH HIM.
cards: It starts with flattery, thick as honey. Teacher, we know you're honest, you don't care what anyone thinks, you teach God's way truly.
The speakers are some Pharisees with some Herodians, a party named for Herod's family; some readers find it an odd pairing. Mark says they were sent to catch him in his words.
Then the question: is it lawful to pay the tax to Caesar, or not? It's a neat trap. Say yes, and he sounds like Rome's man.
Say no, and he sounds like a rebel, with Herodians standing right there. Neither answer looks safe. So Jesus asks for something small.

teach.b: In the King James Bible, he says: "bring me a penny, that I may see it." The penny was a denarius, a silver coin; in another of Jesus's parables, it's a day's pay for a laborer.
He asks them for one, and they bring it, right there in the temple courts.
Then the question: "Whose is this image and superscription?" Image and inscription. They answer: "Caesar's."
The coin carries the emperor's face and his words. Then the line: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And Mark says they marveled at him.
Some readers hear something folded inside it. The same word, image, appears in the Bible's first chapter, where God makes human beings in his own image.

teach.h: GIVE CAESAR WHAT BEARS HIS FACE.
teach.b: So if a coin with Caesar's face belongs to Caesar, give it back to him.
And what does Genesis say carries God's image? Every person.

teach.h: RENDER TO CAESAR THE THINGS THAT ARE CAESAR'S, AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.
teach.b: Jesus doesn't spell that out; readers hear it. Caesar gets the coin; the person belongs to God. Christians have drawn different practical conclusions from this line.
Some hear a clear line between church and state. Others hear a limit on what any government can claim. Others pay their taxes and also say that conscience belongs to God alone.
What they share is the picture: a face on a coin, a face in the mirror, and the question of whose each one is.

how: Christians often quote "render to Caesar" in discussions of faith, taxes and government, and some teach from Genesis 1:27 that every person bears God's image and so deserves dignity.

o: a silver denarius bearing the emperor's face
a temple coin used to pay the priests
a gold coin minted for King Herod's court

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus pulled a coin from his own purse
he asked them to bring one. they had it, in the temple courts.
they answered that the image was Caesar's
"Caesar's." so: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.
image here echoes Genesis, where people are made in God's image
the coin bears Caesar's face; you bear God's.

games.q: you're asked in front of a crowd: should we pay the tax to Caesar, or not? yes makes you a collaborator; no makes you a rebel. what do you do?
o: ask for a coin, and ask whose image is on it.
games.why: he asks for a penny: "Whose is this image and superscription?" then: give Caesar what is Caesar's, and God what is God's. and they marveled.

practice: If you have a coin or a bill nearby, hold it and look at the face on it, or just picture one; then think of your own face, the one the Bible says carries God's image.
What in your day belongs to Caesar, the bills and the job and the rules, and what belongs only to God? If you pray, you can offer that part back.

wordCard.voice: Caesar's coin. A denarius with the emperor's face: give it to Caesar, and give to God what bears God's image.

orig.note: Greek: image, likeness. the root of the English icon. the same word the Greek Bible uses in Genesis 1:27.

carryVoice: Your line: you bear god's image. Caesar gets the coin; the person belongs to God. Day two hundred eleven.
